summary: A Stanford HAI news article reports on research by Vinod Menon and Percy Mistry, who trained a deep neural network to recognize numbers to test whether human number sense is innate or learned. They tested whether 'spontaneous number neurons' in an object-recognition network help with number learning and found they did not, suggesting an innate number sense may be less important than proposed. The network also developed number-line representations resembling those in children, and the team plans to use it to study dyscalculia.
one_line: Stanford researchers used a deep neural network to test whether human number sense is innate or learned, with implications for understanding dyscalculia.
key_facts: Vinod Menon is a Stanford professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and a member of Stanford HAI and the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute.
Percy Mistry is a research scholar in Menon's lab.
The research results were published in Nature Communications.
A previous study found that some neurons in a deep neural network trained to recognize images were sensitive to numbers, responding strongly to pictures of a particular number of objects.
Mistry, Menon, and colleagues found that the spontaneous number neurons did not help the network learn number tasks.
Most neurons that started out number-sensitive either lost that sensitivity during training or became sensitive to a different number.
Removing the number-sensitive neurons during the learning process had no effect on the network's final performance.
The starting object-recognition network had previously been shown to resemble parts of the monkey visual system.

The network used two strategies to tell numbers apart: a linear number line where 1 and 9 were easy to distinguish, and a midpoint-based strategy where 4, 5, and 6 were perceived as very different from each other.
Children also start sensitive to low and high numbers and later use the midpoint of the number line as a reference point.
Menon has spent years studying dyscalculia, a disability that affects numerical and mathematical skills.
Mistry described the model as 'a very, very simple approximation of what the brain is doing, even with all its complexity.'
Mistry said of the model: 'We can use this model as a sandbox.'
The article is written by Grace Huckins and dated July 13, 2023.
